That morning was not the first time I had thought I was going to die.

book_titles.BY_genre_line: A mystical crime and psychological thriller

address_forms.Abi: abi (loanword, never ‘brother’/‘bro’). Capital when attached to a name: ‘Sefa Abi’, ‘Nazım Abi’ (SA [336], [843]); lower case as a bare vocative inside a sentence (‘…, abi.’); capital only sentence-initially (“Abi, are you Nazım Efendi?”). Vocative ‘abim’ → ‘abi’, the possessive being untranslatable: SA [696] ‘my love was made whole, Mustafa Sefa abi’.
address_forms.Hoca: hoca (loanword, never ‘Professor Hakan’/‘teacher’). Capital when attached to a name: ‘Hakan Hoca’; lower case as a common noun: SA [1349] ‘someone people call hoca’.
address_forms.Hocam: hocam (loanword, kept everywhere, never ‘sir’/‘Professor’/‘teacher’). Lower case as a bare vocative inside a sentence — SA has it so 48×, including the canteen man’s generic politeness at [1670] (‘That side has come loose, hocam.’) — capital only sentence-initially (“Hocam, …”) or attached to a name: ‘Sefa Hocam’ (SA [47]). Kept even in SA [73] (“just don’t call me hocam, call me whatever else you like”), since the book’s play with the title depends on the word itself.
address_forms.Amca: amca (loanword). Capital attached to a name: ‘Muhibbi Amca’; possessive forms ‘Muhibbi Amcam/Amcan’ → ‘my/your Muhibbi Amca’ (SA [651]/[765] signature: ‘your Muhibbi Amca’); lower case as a bare vocative inside a sentence.
address_forms.Hanım: Hanım (kept after the name: ‘Vildan Hanım’, ‘Zehra Hanım’; not ‘Mrs’/‘Ms’)
address_forms.Bey: Bey (kept after the name: ‘Sefa Bey’, ‘Nihat Bey’; not ‘Mr’)
address_forms.Evlat: translated, not a loanword: ‘son’ / ‘my boy’ (SA [651] ‘May God accept it, son’); kinship vocatives that are not honorific titles are translated.
the Prophet (before Muhammad: ‘the Prophet Muhammad’); the Archangel (before Azrael/Michael); omitted before other prophets and companions (Hz. Âdem → Adam, Hz. Ebu Bekir → Abu Bakr); never ‘Hazrat’/‘St’
Professor (British usage drops the doubled title: ‘Professor Hakan Hıdıroğlu’, ‘Professor Hakikat Medeni’)

exonyms.Âdemoğlu / Âdemoğulları: the son of Adam / the sons of Adam
exonyms.Belam Bin Baura: Bal‘am ibn Ba‘ura (glossary gloss: the Balaam of the Bible; the gloss stays in the glossary, not in the text)
exonyms.Allah: God in narration and in all Turkish-language speech, blessings and idioms: ‘Allah kabul etsin’ → ‘May God accept it’, ‘maazallah’ → ‘God forbid’, ‘Allah dostu’ → ‘a friend of God’, ‘Allah aşkına’ → ‘for God’s sake’, ‘Allah bilir’ → ‘God knows’, SA [473] ‘aklı veren de Allah, alan da Allah’ → ‘God gives the mind and God takes it’. Allah is kept only inside Arabic-language formulas and quoted Arabic prayer: ‘Allahu akbar’, ‘inshallah’, ‘mashallah’ (maşallah), ‘alhamdulillah’ (Elhamdülillah), ‘Bismillah’. The boundary is linguistic (Arabic formula → Allah; Turkish sentence → God), so the two translators cannot split.

notes:
Spelling and punctuation: British (tumour, colour, fibre, grey, -ise), double quotation marks “ ” for speech, single ‘ ’ for quotes within quotes and for cited sentences. Apostrophes are always typographic ’ (U+2019), also inside the fixed sentences (‘I’m’ in the Bazen line); the pipeline must not normalise them to a straight apostrophe, and translators copy the fixed sentences character for character rather than retyping them. The pipeline check is case-sensitive and matches each entry as a plain substring of the translated paragraph; every decision below was made with the exact surrounding sentences of both books in view, and every Turkish occurrence whose first letter is a capital (sentence-initial or a heading) is a checked paragraph.
1. ‘Öleceğimi ilk kez o sabah düşünmedim.’ → ‘That morning was not the first time I had thought I was going to die.’ Opens both novels (BY [37], SA [1360]) and recurs at BY [3443]. The negation stays on ‘first time’, which is what the Turkish denies. ‘Öleceğimi düşünmek’ is the thought that I was going to die, a future certainty, not the generic contemplation of death (‘ölümü düşünmek’) that BY [38] sets the narrator apart from (‘People think about death. … Mine was not a thought.’); ‘was going to’ is picked up by BY [39] ‘Gidecektim.’ → ‘I was going to go.’ and SA [1361] ‘he had thought of his death before I had’. ‘thought’ stays available for the ‘Mine was not a thought’ echo. No contraction, so the first line lands with full weight; ‘thought I would die’ is avoided because of the ‘would die laughing’ idiom.
2. ‘Kapıyı açtım. İçeri girecek adamın adını henüz bilmiyorum.’ → ‘I opened the door. I do not yet know the name of the man who will come in.’ A writer’s working note (BY [522], [3201]; SA [1363]); past ‘opened’ + present ‘do not yet know’ reproduces the tense shift; uncontracted, so no apostrophe can break the check, and in step with the uncontracted opening line. ‘will come in’ renders ‘girecek’ without adding imminence (BY [3442] paraphrases it as ‘a man whose name he did not yet know’ → ‘He brought to that door a man whose name he did not yet know.’). In BY [3201] the preceding clause must use ‘opened’ as well (‘I opened the cover of the first file. I opened the door.’) to keep the açtım/açtım echo.
3. ‘Okurken hangi elinle tuttuğunu kontrol et.’ → ‘As you read, check which hand you are holding it in.’ Imperative note (SA [1323], BY [2801]); the implied object is the sheet/page (SA [1323] ‘Write this line with your own hand’, BY [2802] ‘Now my hand was holding both of them’), and British idiom for a page or book is ‘hold it in your hand’. BY [2802] contrasts it with the shorter line ‘Okurken eline de bak’ → ‘As you read, look at your hand too.’ so the ‘long sentence / shorter one’ contrast survives.
4. ‘seni ikinci kez öldürmüş gibi oluruz’ → ‘it would be as though we had killed you a second time’. Fragment designed to follow a conditional head clause in both places: ‘If it became a duty, the day we fell silent it would be as though we had killed you a second time.’ (BY [3170] in speech, SA [1735] recalled as ‘a woman’s words’). ‘a second time’ is the one rendering of ‘ikinci kez’ in both books (never ‘for the second time’, ‘again’, ‘twice’), because SA builds a leitmotif on the same words: ‘Bunu ikinci kez yaşıyoruz.’ → ‘We are living this a second time.’ (SA [934], [940]–[942], [1608], [1675]; [1024] ‘Someone is saying we are living this a second time’; [1034] ‘I wrote the sentence “We are living this a second time” in my notebook’), and the note at SA [1681] quotes the bare phrase: ‘“A second time”: my own voice, meaning unclear.’ — a substring of the sentence, as in the Turkish.
5. ‘Bazen onları ben yazmıyorum gibi geliyor’ → ‘Sometimes it feels as if I’m not the one writing them’. Spoken in SA [1698], written as a note in BY [3203]; the contraction suits both speech and a marginal note and is kept (apostrophe U+2019, see header). Followed in both by ‘Ben sustuğumda da odalarında konuşuyorlar.’ → ‘Even when I fall silent, they go on talking in their rooms.’
6. Motto ‘İnsan hakikati öğrenmez, hatırlar’ → ‘Man does not learn the truth; he remembers it’ (motto field with the exclamation mark). Generic ‘Man’ is required because at SA [473] the Devil says it about humankind (‘we’/‘you’ would be wrong in his mouth), and the archaic generic suits an aphorism attributed to Ibn Arabi (SA [39], [361]). Semicolon instead of the Turkish comma avoids a comma splice while keeping one breath; the entry carries no final punctuation so ‘!’ (SA [40], [362], [473], [705], [1540]; BY [3382]) or a comma (SA [1714]) can be appended.
7. ‘Metale üç kez vuruluyor, sonra biri su istiyordu’ → ‘Three knocks on metal, then someone asking for water’. Capitalised, because the only checked occurrence, BY [989], is a free-standing sentence between two others, and the English must keep that three-sentence rhythm: ‘Another of my notes took us to the page that described an old sound recording. Three knocks on metal, then someone asking for water. I also remembered knocking three times on the table as I read.’ SA [1324] has the Turkish in lower case mid-sentence (after ‘Sahnedeki kayıtta’) and is therefore not a checked paragraph; it takes the identical words in lower case: ‘The recording in the scene held three knocks on metal, then someone asking for water.’ — the capital/lower-case split mirrors the Turkish one to one. The participle ‘asking’ keeps the open-ended imperfect ‘istiyordu’ and the echo of SA [1668] ‘No voice asked for water.’ ‘knocks’ is the motif word throughout and must be used wherever the sound recurs: SA chapter title ÜÇ VURUŞ → ‘Three Knocks’, SA [1665] ‘üç metal ses’ → ‘the three metal knocks’, [1667] ‘o üç vuruş’ → ‘those three knocks’, [1681] ‘Üç vuruş: muhtemelen tepsi ve masa.’ → ‘Three knocks: probably tray and table.’, BY [989] ‘knocking three times on the table’; the onomatopoeia at SA [1666] stays ‘tak, tak, tak’. The sound is later explained (SA [1666]–[1681]) as a tray set on the loose metal edge of a garden table, which is the scale ‘knocks’ keeps.
8. ‘Kırılmış.’ → ‘Broken.’ SA [1326] leaves open whether the word is said of a faulty tool or of the hurt person opposite (kırılmak = to break / to be hurt; SA [1328] ‘I did not write whether he said the first word to the tool or to the person opposite’); ‘Broken.’ keeps both readings. The companion line ‘Kapak.’ (SA-only fixed sentence, SA [1327]) → ‘Cap.’: the object in front of the second speaker is an empty glass (SA [1328], BY [3450] ‘the hand trying to pass the glass without dropping it’), so the word is the cap of a bottle; one flat word, as in the Turkish; ‘Lid.’ is withdrawn. BY [3451]/[3452] are not checked paragraphs (comma, not full stop) but carry the identical words in comma form: “Broken,” I said. / “Cap,” I said. BY [3453] then reads ‘Words from two different places. In one there was a person, in the other a thing that had broken.’ — ‘broken’ stays available for the person.
9. ‘siyah paket’ → ‘black parcel’: an unmarked, matt-black-paper-wrapped delivery left at a door (BY [169], [324]); British ‘parcel’ is exact and gives the chapter title ‘2. The Black Parcel’. SA [1694]: ‘A door, a black parcel, a red string, a man with his right thumb taped.’
10. ‘kırmızı ip’ → ‘red string’: thin enough for a child’s wrist (BY [65]), a chair arm and a door handle, strong enough to tie a parcel at four corners (BY [169]); it is the ‘red string of fate’ and the Kabbalistic red string in BY [171]. In BY [171] the paragraph argues that it is the same ‘ip’ across the Greek, East Asian and Jewish stories, so Ariadne keeps her established ‘thread’ but is bridged to the fixed word: ‘Ariadne’s thread, a string whose colour did not matter, led Theseus back out of the labyrinth. The red string of fate in Chinese and Japanese folk tales bound with an invisible tie the people whose paths were going to cross. In some Jewish folk traditions the red string was tied to the wrist against the evil eye and ill luck; even within that tradition its religious source was disputed. The same string could show the way, bind, or, if the knot was pulled too tight, cut off movement.’ The BY knot sentence ‘Düğümün iki ucu aynı uzunluktaydı’ → ‘The two ends of the knot were the same length.’
11. ‘Tümör’ → ‘Tumour’: the word on the report at BY [3439] (one-word paragraph: ‘Tumour.’). All three SA occurrences are capitalised in the Turkish and are therefore checked paragraphs; each must contain capital ‘Tumour’ as an exact substring, and each is given here in natural English: SA [1349] keeps the Turkish ‘cümle’ a sentence: “I heard the sentence ‘Tumour is a possibility’, then other words as well: further investigation, location, treatment options.” SA [1658] opens the doctor’s speech with the clinical mass-noun phrase: “Tumour location is consistent with the change in your speech over recent months and with your growing withdrawal into yourself. We regard the tumour as the main cause of these changes,” the doctor said. “But we cannot explain your other perceptual experiences with a single finding; those need to be assessed separately.” SA [1694] sets the word on its own, as on the report at BY [3439]: ‘Tumour. I put in front of him the notebook from the night that word had arrived. A door, a black parcel, a red string, a man with his right thumb taped. Another life, built on a white page.’ Everywhere else ordinary lower-case ‘tumour’ (second mention in [1658], SA [1354] ‘the one word I had heard’).
12. Names: all fictional characters and Istanbul places keep their Turkish spelling and diacritics (Hıdıroğlu, Erenköy, Kadıköy, Nazım, Tarık, Duru, Nehir, Meralis, Hakikat Medeni — the pun on ‘truth’ is noted in the SA glossary but not translated). Only ‘Istanbul’ takes the English form. Scriptural and historical figures and places take their established English forms (see exonyms); this now includes the Qur’anic/tafsir figure of SA [1153]–[1172]: ‘Belam Bin Baura’ → ‘Bal‘am ibn Ba‘ura’, short form ‘Belam’ → ‘Bal‘am’ (the Balaam of the Bible; the gloss belongs in the glossary, not in the Devil’s speech), because the Moses/Red Sea context ([1158]) makes the figure recognisable and ‘Belam’ next to ‘Moses’ would be inconsistent. Hanzeb, Balakt, Mabeh are invented demonic names with no English tradition and stay as they are. The cat Duman and the nickname Küçük Saatçi are BY-bible decisions (recommend ‘Duman’ unchanged, ‘the Little Watchmaker’ translated).
13. Honorifics, one rule for all loanword titles (abi, hoca, hocam, amca, hanım, bey, efendi), as in current British translations of Turkish fiction: capital when attached to a name (Sefa Abi, Nazım Abi, Hakan Hoca, Sefa Hocam, Muhibbi Amca, Vildan Hanım, Sefa Bey, Nazım Efendi); lower case as a bare vocative inside a sentence (‘…, abi.’, ‘…, hocam.’, ‘…, amca.’); capital only sentence-initially (“Abi, are you Nazım Efendi?”). Possessive vocatives lose the suffix: ‘abim’ → ‘abi’ (SA [696] ‘my love was made whole, Mustafa Sefa abi’), ‘Muhibbi Amcan’ → ‘your Muhibbi Amca’. ‘hocam’ is kept even where the title is refused or generic: SA [73] “just don’t call me hocam, call me whatever else you like” and the canteen man at [1670] — the book’s play with the title depends on the word. ‘evlat’ is not a title and is translated (‘son’). One glossary line per book suffices.
14. Book titles as fixed by the brief: THE TRAVELLER (British double l) and THE WITNESS; BY subtitle ‘1453 — The Price of Awakening’ (BY [3199] ‘I named it 1453 — The Price of Awakening’); BY genre line ‘A mystical crime and psychological thriller’ (English blurb phrasing; ‘mystical crime novel’ read as crime committed by mystics). MARK ‘14.53 ↺’ stays untranslated.
15. Cross-book signposts to the two titles: ‘yolcu’ meaning the addressee → ‘traveller’ (never wayfarer/pilgrim/passenger), SA [38] ‘Remember, traveller: you are setting out now on the real journey, and the road awaits you, and so does the witness… Remember, because:’; ‘yolculuk’ → ‘journey’ (SA [3] ‘the journey of a short, upright life’). ‘şahit’ (SA throughout) and ‘tanık’ (BY [988]) → ‘witness’ in both books (never testimony/observer/bystander); BY [2685] ‘Şahit ol’ → ‘Bear witness’; SA [3] ‘Şahit eden’ → ‘made us witnesses’; SA [1714] ‘başkasının tanıklığına’ → ‘someone else’s witness’.
16. Allah/God: the boundary is linguistic, see exonyms — Arabic formulas keep Allah (Allahu akbar, inshallah, mashallah, alhamdulillah, Bismillah), Turkish-language sentences, blessings and idioms take God (‘May God accept it’, ‘God forbid’, ‘a friend of God’, ‘God gives the mind and God takes it’ at SA [473]).
17. Final editorial decisions on the critics’ objections (shared_en_issues.json and the second list). Accepted: Tümör at SA [1694] added with a capitalised opening (high); [1658] and [1349] rewritten as grammatical sentences (‘Tumour location is consistent with…’, ‘Tumour is a possibility’); opening line changed to ‘thought I was going to die’ (future certainty of Öleceğim, BY [39]); Metale capitalised as a verbless sentence with ‘knocks’ cross-references; apostrophe rule added and the Kapıyı açtım line made contraction-free (‘I do not yet know … who will come in’); Belam → Bal‘am ibn Ba‘ura / Bal‘am with glossary gloss; Kapak → ‘Cap.’ and BY [3451]/[3452] comma forms; one capitalisation rule for all honorific loanwords, hocam kept at SA [73] and [1670]; ‘a second time’ fixed for the SA leitmotif and [1681]; ‘holding it in’; genre line ‘A mystical crime and psychological thriller’; traveller/witness signposts (with the correction that ‘Yolculuğuna’ in SA [3] is ‘journey’, not ‘traveller’); Ariadne bridge ‘Ariadne’s thread, a string whose colour did not matter’; Allah/God linguistic boundary. Rejected: ‘thought of dying’ for the opening line (shorter, but it keeps the generic ‘contemplating death’ reading that BY [38] explicitly rejects; the semantic objection outweighs the cadence objection); the finite passive ‘metal was struck three times, then someone was asking for water’ (loses the motif word ‘knocks’ shared with the chapter title and SA [1665]–[1681], and reads as flat English; the imperfect is carried by ‘asking’); removing the contraction from the Bazen line (spoken dialogue in SA [1698]; the risk is covered by the apostrophe rule instead).
